items.stem: Which result, if observed after extending the experiment beyond the time shown in Figure 1, would support the model's prediction about the eventual endpoint concentration?
choices: The TiO2 and no-TiO2 samples eventually reach the same dye concentration.
The two samples still have different concentrations at 15 minutes.
The TiO2 sample has a lower concentration during the first 15 minutes.
The no-TiO2 sample's concentration decreases during the 15-minute interval.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested a model of titanium dioxide (TiO2) photocatalysis by measuring the disappearance rate of an aqueous dye at several blue-light irradiances, with and without TiO2. The model predicts that TiO2 will increase the degradation rate at any nonzero irradiance but that TiO2 and the control will have equal rates in complete darkness. It also predicts that TiO2 changes the rate of degradation but not the eventual endpoint concentration, and a more specific version predicts that doubling irradiance from 20 to 40 mW/cm² will double the TiO2-catalyzed rate. Table 1 gives measured initial rates, and Figure 1 follows dye concentration for 15 minutes at 40 mW/cm².
items.explanation: The model predicts that TiO2 changes the rate but not the eventual endpoint concentration. Therefore, convergence to the same concentration after a sufficiently long exposure would support that prediction.

per_choice.correct: The model predicts that TiO2 changes the rate but not the eventual endpoint concentration. Therefore, convergence to the same concentration after a sufficiently long exposure would support that prediction.
per_choice.trap: Choices B, C, and D describe observations already shown in Figure 1, but they do not test the eventual endpoint after the displayed interval.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, at 2 g/L salt, which measurement showed the greater percentage reduction relative to the 0 g/L treatment?
choices: The number of germinated seeds, because it decreased from 20 to 19.
Mean final root length, because it decreased from 5.0 cm to 4.3 cm.
The two measurements showed equal percentage reductions.
The comparison cannot be made because the measurements use different units.
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seeds for 6 days in solutions containing different salt concentrations and measured germination and root growth. They proposed a model in which increasing salinity reduces both processes, with each additional 2 g/L of salt removing the same number of germinated seeds. Table 1 gives germination results, Figure 1 shows mean root length during the experiment, and Figure 2 shows mean root length after seedlings were transferred to salt-free solution for 2 days. The same seedlings and salt concentrations are represented across the displays.
items.explanation: The number of germinated seeds decreased by 1 out of 20, or 5 percent. Mean final root length decreased by 0.7 cm out of 5.0 cm, or 14 percent. Thus, mean final root length showed the greater percentage reduction.

per_choice.correct: The number of germinated seeds decreased by 1 out of 20, or 5 percent. Mean final root length decreased by 0.7 cm out of 5.0 cm, or 14 percent. Thus, mean final root length showed the greater percentage reduction.
per_choice.trap: The first choice compares absolute decreases instead of percentage decreases, the third treats unequal percentage changes as equal, and the fourth incorrectly claims that different units prevent percentage comparisons relative to each measurement's own control.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1 regarding the hypothesis that coating reduces mass loss at both temperatures?
choices: The hypothesis is untested because the apples were measured for only 7 days.
The hypothesis is supported only at 20°C because the 30°C coated apples lost more mass than the 20°C uncoated apples.
The hypothesis is contradicted because mass loss increased for coated apples as storage time increased.
The hypothesis is supported because coated apples had less mass loss than uncoated apples at every listed day and temperature.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether a biodegradable coating reduces water loss and preserves firmness in stored apples. Apples were coated or left uncoated and stored at 20°C or 30°C; mass loss was measured after several days. The researchers hypothesized that coating would reduce mass loss under both temperatures and that its advantage would become greater during longer storage at the higher temperature. Firmness measurements for apples stored at 20°C are shown separately in Figure 1.
items.explanation: At every matching day, coated apples had lower mass loss than uncoated apples at both 20°C and 30°C.

per_choice.correct: At every matching day, coated apples had lower mass loss than uncoated apples at both 20°C and 30°C.
per_choice.trap: Choice B compares a coated value at 30°C with an uncoated value at 20°C instead of comparing treatments at the same temperature; choice C reverses the meaning of increasing mass loss over time.

items.stem: The researchers predicted that the coating's reduction in mass loss would be greatest after 7 days at 30°C. Does Table 1 support this prediction?
choices: Yes; the reduction is 6.1 percentage points at 30°C after 7 days, larger than the reductions at the other times and temperature.
Yes; the reduction is 4.3 percentage points at 20°C after 7 days.
No; the reduction is only 1.0 percentage point at 30°C after 1 day.
No; 8.4% is the greatest mass-loss value listed for coated apples.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether a biodegradable coating reduces water loss and preserves firmness in stored apples. Apples were coated or left uncoated and stored at 20°C or 30°C; mass loss was measured after several days. The researchers hypothesized that coating would reduce mass loss under both temperatures and that its advantage would become greater during longer storage at the higher temperature. Firmness measurements for apples stored at 20°C are shown separately in Figure 1.
items.explanation: At 30°C on day 7, the reduction is 14.5% minus 8.4%, or 6.1 percentage points. This exceeds the day-7 reduction at 20°C and all earlier reductions.

per_choice.correct: At 30°C on day 7, the reduction is 14.5% minus 8.4%, or 6.1 percentage points. This exceeds the day-7 reduction at 20°C and all earlier reductions.
per_choice.trap: Choice B uses the correct day but the lower-temperature comparison; choice D treats the coated value as the treatment difference rather than subtracting it from the uncoated value.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: The researchers also hypothesized that coating preserves firmness during storage at 20°C. Which statement best evaluates this hypothesis using Figure 1?
choices: It is untested because Figure 1 reports firmness rather than mass loss.
It is supported only at day 4 because both types had the same firmness at day 0.
It is supported because coated apples were firmer than uncoated apples on both day 4 and day 7, with the gap increasing over time.
It is contradicted because firmness decreased for both types of apples from day 0 to day 7.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether a biodegradable coating reduces water loss and preserves firmness in stored apples. Apples were coated or left uncoated and stored at 20°C or 30°C; mass loss was measured after several days. The researchers hypothesized that coating would reduce mass loss under both temperatures and that its advantage would become greater during longer storage at the higher temperature. Firmness measurements for apples stored at 20°C are shown separately in Figure 1.
items.explanation: Figure 1 shows coated apples at 15 N versus 12 N on day 4 and 13 N versus 8 N on day 7; the coated apples remain firmer and the difference grows.

items.stem: Which additional claim would remain untested by the results in Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: The coating preserves greater firmness than no coating at 20°C by day 7.
The coating reduces mass loss at 30°C during the first 7 days.
The coating reduces mass loss at 20°C during the first 7 days.
The coating will continue to preserve firmness after 14 days of storage.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested whether a biodegradable coating reduces water loss and preserves firmness in stored apples. Apples were coated or left uncoated and stored at 20°C or 30°C; mass loss was measured after several days. The researchers hypothesized that coating would reduce mass loss under both temperatures and that its advantage would become greater during longer storage at the higher temperature. Firmness measurements for apples stored at 20°C are shown separately in Figure 1.
items.explanation: The longest storage time shown in either display is 7 days, so the effect after 14 days was not measured.

per_choice.correct: The longest storage time shown in either display is 7 days, so the effect after 14 days was not measured.

items.stem: According to the experiment summarized in Table 1, what hypothesis was being tested?
choices: Longer light exposure increases algal oxygen production.
Algae grow best in salty water.
Higher water temperature decreases algal oxygen production.
Algae produce oxygen only during darkness.
items.stimulus: Researchers studied whether longer light exposure increases oxygen production by freshwater algae. Their hypothesis was that cultures exposed to light for more hours each day would produce more oxygen. They placed equal-sized algal cultures under different daily light durations and measured oxygen production after 7 days. Table 1 reports the measurements and the assessment of the hypothesis.
items.explanation: The passage states that the hypothesis was that cultures exposed to light for more hours would produce more oxygen.

per_choice.correct: The passage states that the hypothesis was that cultures exposed to light for more hours would produce more oxygen.
per_choice.trap: The other choices refer to temperature, darkness, or salinity, none of which was the stated hypothesis.

items.stem: Which conclusion about the hypothesis is best supported when the final biomass in Table 1 and the oxygen trends in Figure 1 are considered together?
choices: The hypothesis is untested because the cultures began with equal biomass.
The hypothesis is contradicted because nitrate increased final biomass under both light conditions.
The hypothesis is supported only for oxygen production, because biomass was greater in every high-light treatment.
The hypothesis is supported because nitrate had a much larger effect under high light than under low light in both measurements.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested the hypothesis that nitrate increases algal growth only when light intensity is high enough to provide energy for nitrate assimilation. Algal cultures were grown for 7 days with or without added nitrate under low or high light, and biomass and dissolved oxygen were measured. The hypothesis predicts little difference between nitrate treatments under low light but larger nitrate-associated increases under high light. Table 1 gives biomass measurements, while Figure 1 shows dissolved oxygen during the experiment.
items.explanation: In Table 1, nitrate changes final biomass only slightly at low light (2.3 to 2.4) but substantially at high light (3.1 to 4.8). Figure 1 shows the same pattern for oxygen: nitrate has little effect at low light but a larger effect at high light.

per_choice.correct: In Table 1, nitrate changes final biomass only slightly at low light (2.3 to 2.4) but substantially at high light (3.1 to 4.8). Figure 1 shows the same pattern for oxygen: nitrate has little effect at low light but a larger effect at high light.
per_choice.trap: A reader may focus on the small low-light increase or on the fact that all high-light cultures grew, rather than comparing the nitrate effect within each light level in both displays.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which inference cannot be made from Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: The large nitrate-associated increase occurred under high light.
Nitrate is necessary for any growth or oxygen production under high light.
The treatment with high light and nitrate produced the greatest final biomass and oxygen level.
The nitrate effect on both measured outcomes was small under low light.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested the hypothesis that nitrate increases algal growth only when light intensity is high enough to provide energy for nitrate assimilation. Algal cultures were grown for 7 days with or without added nitrate under low or high light, and biomass and dissolved oxygen were measured. The hypothesis predicts little difference between nitrate treatments under low light but larger nitrate-associated increases under high light. Table 1 gives biomass measurements, while Figure 1 shows dissolved oxygen during the experiment.
items.explanation: High-light cultures without nitrate still increased from 2.0 to 3.1 mg/L biomass and from 6.2 to 8.0 mg/L oxygen. Therefore, nitrate was not necessary for all high-light growth or oxygen production, even though it increased both outcomes.

per_choice.correct: High-light cultures without nitrate still increased from 2.0 to 3.1 mg/L biomass and from 6.2 to 8.0 mg/L oxygen. Therefore, nitrate was not necessary for all high-light growth or oxygen production, even though it increased both outcomes.
per_choice.trap: A reader may interpret the high-light nitrate treatment as showing that nitrate is required, confusing the largest response with the only response.

items.stem: Which statement identifies a limitation in what the agreement between Table 1 and Figure 1 demonstrates about the proposed model?
choices: The data show that high light without nitrate produced more biomass and oxygen than low light with nitrate.
The data show that low-light cultures responded similarly whether nitrate was present or absent.
The data show that high light with nitrate produced the highest biomass and oxygen level.
The data do not establish that light enables nitrate assimilation as the mechanism; they show only that the two measured outcomes respond in the predicted pattern.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested the hypothesis that nitrate increases algal growth only when light intensity is high enough to provide energy for nitrate assimilation. Algal cultures were grown for 7 days with or without added nitrate under low or high light, and biomass and dissolved oxygen were measured. The hypothesis predicts little difference between nitrate treatments under low light but larger nitrate-associated increases under high light. Table 1 gives biomass measurements, while Figure 1 shows dissolved oxygen during the experiment.
items.explanation: Both displays support the predicted interaction between light and nitrate, but neither directly measures nitrate assimilation or proves that it causes the observed changes. The displays establish an outcome pattern, not the mechanism proposed to explain it.

per_choice.correct: Both displays support the predicted interaction between light and nitrate, but neither directly measures nitrate assimilation or proves that it causes the observed changes. The displays establish an outcome pattern, not the mechanism proposed to explain it.
per_choice.trap: A reader may treat agreement between biomass and oxygen as proof of the biological mechanism, even though both are indirect outcome measurements.

items.stem: Which evaluation of the model is best supported by Table 1?
choices: The model is fully supported because TiO2 gives a higher rate at every irradiance.
The model is supported for nonzero irradiance but contradicted by the unequal dark-condition rates.
The model is untested because the table reports rates rather than final dye concentrations.
The model is fully contradicted because the control also degrades dye at nonzero irradiance.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested a model of titanium dioxide (TiO2) photocatalysis by measuring the disappearance rate of an aqueous dye at several blue-light irradiances, with and without TiO2. The model predicts that TiO2 will increase the degradation rate at any nonzero irradiance but that TiO2 and the control will have equal rates in complete darkness. It also predicts that TiO2 changes the rate of degradation but not the eventual endpoint concentration, and a more specific version predicts that doubling irradiance from 20 to 40 mW/cm² will double the TiO2-catalyzed rate. Table 1 gives measured initial rates, and Figure 1 follows dye concentration for 15 minutes at 40 mW/cm².
items.explanation: At 20, 40, and 60 mW/cm², the TiO2 rate exceeds the control rate, supporting the light-dependent prediction. At 0 mW/cm², the rates are 0.8 and 0.7 rather than equal, contradicting the model's dark-condition prediction.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which prediction of the model remains untested by the results in Figure 1?
choices: The two samples have different concentrations after 15 minutes.
TiO2 and no TiO2 eventually reach the same endpoint concentration.
TiO2 lowers the dye concentration more rapidly during the first 15 minutes.
The no-TiO2 sample undergoes some degradation at 40 mW/cm².
items.stimulus: Researchers tested a model of titanium dioxide (TiO2) photocatalysis by measuring the disappearance rate of an aqueous dye at several blue-light irradiances, with and without TiO2. The model predicts that TiO2 will increase the degradation rate at any nonzero irradiance but that TiO2 and the control will have equal rates in complete darkness. It also predicts that TiO2 changes the rate of degradation but not the eventual endpoint concentration, and a more specific version predicts that doubling irradiance from 20 to 40 mW/cm² will double the TiO2-catalyzed rate. Table 1 gives measured initial rates, and Figure 1 follows dye concentration for 15 minutes at 40 mW/cm².
items.explanation: The model's endpoint prediction concerns what happens after sufficiently long exposure. Figure 1 ends at 15 minutes, when the concentrations are still different, so it neither establishes nor rules out eventual convergence.

per_choice.correct: The model's endpoint prediction concerns what happens after sufficiently long exposure. Figure 1 ends at 15 minutes, when the concentrations are still different, so it neither establishes nor rules out eventual convergence.

items.stem: How do the results in Table 1 evaluate the model's specific prediction that doubling irradiance from 20 to 40 mW/cm² will double the TiO2-catalyzed rate?
choices: The prediction is contradicted exactly because the rate increases by more than twofold.
The prediction is untested because the 20 and 40 mW/cm² measurements come from different samples.
The prediction is supported exactly because the rate increases from 4.0 to 7.2 mg/L/min.
The qualitative increase is supported, but the exact doubling prediction is not: the rate increases by a factor of 1.8.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested a model of titanium dioxide (TiO2) photocatalysis by measuring the disappearance rate of an aqueous dye at several blue-light irradiances, with and without TiO2. The model predicts that TiO2 will increase the degradation rate at any nonzero irradiance but that TiO2 and the control will have equal rates in complete darkness. It also predicts that TiO2 changes the rate of degradation but not the eventual endpoint concentration, and a more specific version predicts that doubling irradiance from 20 to 40 mW/cm² will double the TiO2-catalyzed rate. Table 1 gives measured initial rates, and Figure 1 follows dye concentration for 15 minutes at 40 mW/cm².
items.explanation: For TiO2, the rate changes from 4.0 to 7.2 mg/L/min. The ratio is 7.2 ÷ 4.0 = 1.8, so the rate increases as predicted but does not double exactly.

per_choice.correct: For TiO2, the rate changes from 4.0 to 7.2 mg/L/min. The ratio is 7.2 ÷ 4.0 = 1.8, so the rate increases as predicted but does not double exactly.
per_choice.trap: Choice C treats any increase as an exact doubling; choice A reverses the comparison and calls a less-than-twofold increase greater than twofold; choice B ignores that both irradiances are explicitly reported for the TiO2 condition.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which conclusion best evaluates the hypothesis using Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2?
choices: The hypothesis is fully supported because every nitrogen concentration produced measurable growth.
The hypothesis is partly contradicted because increasing nitrogen from 50 to 75 mg/L did not increase height or flower number and slightly decreased chlorophyll.
The hypothesis is fully contradicted because plants receiving 25 mg/L were shorter than plants receiving 50 mg/L.
The hypothesis is untested because the plants were not exposed to nitrogen concentrations below 0 mg/L.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested the hypothesis that increasing nitrogen fertilizer concentration from 0 to 75 mg/L would increase bean-plant growth at every concentration. Plants were grown under identical light, water, and soil conditions, and nitrogen concentration was the variable changed. Table 1 shows mean plant height after 14 days, Figure 1 shows mean leaf chlorophyll index, and Figure 2 shows mean number of flowers per plant. All three displays use nitrogen concentration as the independent variable.
items.explanation: The hypothesis predicts an increase at every step. From 50 to 75 mg/L, height remains 23 cm, flowers remain at 6 per plant, and chlorophyll decreases from 41 to 40.

per_choice.correct: The hypothesis predicts an increase at every step. From 50 to 75 mg/L, height remains 23 cm, flowers remain at 6 per plant, and chlorophyll decreases from 41 to 40.
per_choice.trap: The tempting error is to treat the increases from 0 to 50 mg/L as evidence that the entire hypothesis is supported, while ignoring the final concentration.

items.stem: When nitrogen concentration was increased from 50 to 75 mg/L, what pattern is shown across Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2?
choices: All three measurements increased.
Height and flower number stayed the same, while chlorophyll index decreased.
Height decreased, chlorophyll index increased, and flower number stayed the same.
Height increased, chlorophyll index stayed the same, and flower number decreased.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested the hypothesis that increasing nitrogen fertilizer concentration from 0 to 75 mg/L would increase bean-plant growth at every concentration. Plants were grown under identical light, water, and soil conditions, and nitrogen concentration was the variable changed. Table 1 shows mean plant height after 14 days, Figure 1 shows mean leaf chlorophyll index, and Figure 2 shows mean number of flowers per plant. All three displays use nitrogen concentration as the independent variable.
items.explanation: Table 1 gives heights of 23 cm at both concentrations, Figure 1 drops from 41 to 40, and Figure 2 gives 6 flowers per plant at both concentrations.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 gives heights of 23 cm at both concentrations, Figure 1 drops from 41 to 40, and Figure 2 gives 6 flowers per plant at both concentrations.
per_choice.trap: A student may read the overall upward trend from 0 to 50 mg/L instead of comparing the two requested concentrations.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: A researcher plans to test 100 mg/L and asks which prediction is best supported by the trends in Table 1, Figure 1, and Figure 2. Which prediction is most reasonable?
choices: All three measurements will probably be greater than their 75 mg/L values.
Height and flower number will probably remain near their 75 mg/L values, while chlorophyll will probably not exceed its 50 mg/L value.
Height will probably decrease to the 0 mg/L value, while flower number will probably increase.
Chlorophyll will probably increase sharply, even though height and flower number will probably remain unchanged.
items.stimulus: Researchers tested the hypothesis that increasing nitrogen fertilizer concentration from 0 to 75 mg/L would increase bean-plant growth at every concentration. Plants were grown under identical light, water, and soil conditions, and nitrogen concentration was the variable changed. Table 1 shows mean plant height after 14 days, Figure 1 shows mean leaf chlorophyll index, and Figure 2 shows mean number of flowers per plant. All three displays use nitrogen concentration as the independent variable.
items.explanation: Height and flower number level off between 50 and 75 mg/L, and chlorophyll decreases slightly from 50 to 75 mg/L. These trends best support little additional benefit at 100 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: Height and flower number level off between 50 and 75 mg/L, and chlorophyll decreases slightly from 50 to 75 mg/L. These trends best support little additional benefit at 100 mg/L.
per_choice.trap: The all-increasing prediction extends the early trend from 0 to 50 mg/L and overlooks the leveling or decline at the highest tested concentration.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Considering both Table 1 and Figure 1, which evaluation of the researchers' hypothesis is best supported?
choices: The germination portion is contradicted, but the dry-mass portion is supported because the longest germination time occurred at the highest salt concentration.
The hypothesis is untested because the data do not include a 0 g/L comparison.
The germination portion is supported, but the dry-mass portion is contradicted because mean mass per germinated seed decreased as salinity increased.
The hypothesis is fully supported because increasing salinity lowered germination while leaving seedling dry mass unchanged.
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of bean seedlings. Seeds were placed in solutions containing 0, 2, 4, or 6 g/L sodium chloride, and measurements were made after 10 days. The researchers hypothesized that salinity would reduce the percentage of seeds that germinated but would not affect the dry mass of seedlings that did germinate. Table 1 gives germination results and mean time to germination, Figure 1 gives mean dry mass per germinated seed, and Figure 2 gives the root-to-shoot mass ratio at each salt concentration.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows that germination falls from 96% at 0 g/L to 48% at 6 g/L, supporting the first portion. Figure 1 shows that mean dry mass per germinated seed also falls, from 0.84 g to 0.35 g, contradicting the claim that dry mass would be unaffected.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows that germination falls from 96% at 0 g/L to 48% at 6 g/L, supporting the first portion. Figure 1 shows that mean dry mass per germinated seed also falls, from 0.84 g to 0.35 g, contradicting the claim that dry mass would be unaffected.
per_choice.trap: Choice D treats the decrease in germination as if it also confirmed unchanged mass. Choice A reverses the germination interpretation and uses the time trend as if it were germination percentage. Choice B ignores the 0 g/L control shown in both displays.

items.stem: Using the germination percentages in Table 1 and the per-seed dry masses in Figure 1, how much less total dry mass would be expected from 100 seeds at 4 g/L than from 100 seeds at 0 g/L?
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated how sodium chloride concentration affects the early growth of bean seedlings. Seeds were placed in solutions containing 0, 2, 4, or 6 g/L sodium chloride, and measurements were made after 10 days. The researchers hypothesized that salinity would reduce the percentage of seeds that germinated but would not affect the dry mass of seedlings that did germinate. Table 1 gives germination results and mean time to germination, Figure 1 gives mean dry mass per germinated seed, and Figure 2 gives the root-to-shoot mass ratio at each salt concentration.
items.explanation: At 0 g/L, 96 seeds are expected to germinate, giving 96 × 0.84 = 80.64 g. At 4 g/L, 75 seeds are expected to germinate, giving 75 × 0.61 = 45.75 g. The difference is 80.64 − 45.75 = 34.89 g.

per_choice.correct: At 0 g/L, 96 seeds are expected to germinate, giving 96 × 0.84 = 80.64 g. At 4 g/L, 75 seeds are expected to germinate, giving 75 × 0.61 = 45.75 g. The difference is 80.64 − 45.75 = 34.89 g.
per_choice.trap: 22.08 g results from using the 0 g/L germination percentage with the 4 g/L mass. 45.75 g is only the calculated 4 g/L total, and 80.64 g is only the calculated control total.

items.stimulus: Researchers studied how temperature affects the activity and stability of a catalase enzyme. Equal enzyme samples were tested at several temperatures, and oxygen production was used as a measure of reaction activity. Table 1 lists measured reaction rates, Figure 1 shows oxygen production over time for two temperatures, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of enzyme activity remaining after exposure to each temperature.
items.explanation: The rate is 28 mL O2/min at 40 C and 14 mL O2/min at 60 C, so the difference is 28 − 14 = 14 mL O2/min.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which temperature is best supported by both Table 1 and Figure 2 as providing high reaction activity while preserving the enzyme?
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how temperature affects the activity and stability of a catalase enzyme. Equal enzyme samples were tested at several temperatures, and oxygen production was used as a measure of reaction activity. Table 1 lists measured reaction rates, Figure 1 shows oxygen production over time for two temperatures, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of enzyme activity remaining after exposure to each temperature.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows the highest reaction rate at 40 C, and Figure 2 shows that 96% of activity remains at 40 C.

per_choice.correct: Table 1 shows the highest reaction rate at 40 C, and Figure 2 shows that 96% of activity remains at 40 C.
per_choice.trap: Choosing 50 C uses its relatively high rate from Table 1 but overlooks its much lower remaining activity in Figure 2.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Using Figure 1, by how much does the average oxygen-production rate from 1 to 4 minutes at 50 C exceed the rate at 30 C?
choices: 1.0 mL/min
1.5 mL/min
2.5 mL/min
12.5 mL/min
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how temperature affects the activity and stability of a catalase enzyme. Equal enzyme samples were tested at several temperatures, and oxygen production was used as a measure of reaction activity. Table 1 lists measured reaction rates, Figure 1 shows oxygen production over time for two temperatures, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of enzyme activity remaining after exposure to each temperature.
items.explanation: At 30 C, production increases from 11 to 44 mL over 3 minutes, or 11 mL/min. At 50 C, it increases from 12.5 to 50 mL, or 12.5 mL/min. The difference is 1.5 mL/min.

per_choice.correct: At 30 C, production increases from 11 to 44 mL over 3 minutes, or 11 mL/min. At 50 C, it increases from 12.5 to 50 mL, or 12.5 mL/min. The difference is 1.5 mL/min.
per_choice.trap: Choosing 12.5 uses the 50 C rate without subtracting the 30 C rate.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: A researcher hypothesized that 50 C would produce a faster reaction than 30 C but would leave less enzyme activity remaining. Do the results support this hypothesis? Use Table 1 and Figure 2.
choices: Yes, because the rate is higher at 50 C and the remaining activity is lower.
The hypothesis is contradicted because the two temperatures have the same reaction rate.
The hypothesis is untested because only one of the two temperatures was measured.
No, because the rate is lower at 50 C and the remaining activity is higher.
items.stimulus: Researchers studied how temperature affects the activity and stability of a catalase enzyme. Equal enzyme samples were tested at several temperatures, and oxygen production was used as a measure of reaction activity. Table 1 lists measured reaction rates, Figure 1 shows oxygen production over time for two temperatures, and Figure 2 shows the percentage of enzyme activity remaining after exposure to each temperature.
items.explanation: Table 1 shows a rate of 25 at 50 C versus 22 at 30 C, while Figure 2 shows 62% activity remaining at 50 C versus 91% at 30 C. Both predicted differences occur.

per_choice.trap: Choosing the fourth option reverses both comparisons, while the other options ignore that both temperatures appear in both displays.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Do the germination results in Table 1 support the model's specific prediction that every additional 2 g/L of salt removes the same number of germinated seeds?
choices: No, because the number germinated is unchanged between 4 and 6 g/L.
No, because the successive decreases are 1, 4, and 7 seeds rather than equal decreases.
Yes, because the number germinated decreases at every salt concentration.
Yes, because the mean day of germination increases at every salt concentration.
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seeds for 6 days in solutions containing different salt concentrations and measured germination and root growth. They proposed a model in which increasing salinity reduces both processes, with each additional 2 g/L of salt removing the same number of germinated seeds. Table 1 gives germination results, Figure 1 shows mean root length during the experiment, and Figure 2 shows mean root length after seedlings were transferred to salt-free solution for 2 days. The same seedlings and salt concentrations are represented across the displays.
items.explanation: The numbers germinated are 20, 19, 15, and 8, so the successive losses are 1, 4, and 7 seeds. The direction of the trend supports a salt effect, but the model's specific equal-decrease prediction is not supported.

per_choice.correct: The numbers germinated are 20, 19, 15, and 8, so the successive losses are 1, 4, and 7 seeds. The direction of the trend supports a salt effect, but the model's specific equal-decrease prediction is not supported.
per_choice.trap: Choices C and D confuse general support for a salinity effect with support for the model's more specific equal-decrease prediction; D misreads the 4 and 6 g/L rows.

items.stem: Using Table 1 and Figure 1, at which lowest salt concentration does the percentage reduction in final root length, relative to 0 g/L, exceed the percentage reduction in the number of germinated seeds?
choices: 0 g/L
2 g/L
4 g/L
6 g/L
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seeds for 6 days in solutions containing different salt concentrations and measured germination and root growth. They proposed a model in which increasing salinity reduces both processes, with each additional 2 g/L of salt removing the same number of germinated seeds. Table 1 gives germination results, Figure 1 shows mean root length during the experiment, and Figure 2 shows mean root length after seedlings were transferred to salt-free solution for 2 days. The same seedlings and salt concentrations are represented across the displays.
items.explanation: At 2 g/L, germination falls from 20 to 19, a 5% reduction. Final root length falls from 5.0 cm to 4.3 cm, a 14% reduction. Thus 2 g/L is the lowest concentration at which the root-length reduction is larger.

per_choice.correct: At 2 g/L, germination falls from 20 to 19, a 5% reduction. Final root length falls from 5.0 cm to 4.3 cm, a 14% reduction. Thus 2 g/L is the lowest concentration at which the root-length reduction is larger.
per_choice.trap: Choosing 4 or 6 g/L overlooks that the comparison already holds at 2 g/L; choosing 0 g/L treats the control as having a reduction.

items.stem: For seedlings initially grown at 6 g/L salt, how much did mean root length increase during the 2-day salt-free recovery period, according to Figures 1 and 2?
choices: 1.8 cm
2.4 cm
4.2 cm
6.0 cm
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seeds for 6 days in solutions containing different salt concentrations and measured germination and root growth. They proposed a model in which increasing salinity reduces both processes, with each additional 2 g/L of salt removing the same number of germinated seeds. Table 1 gives germination results, Figure 1 shows mean root length during the experiment, and Figure 2 shows mean root length after seedlings were transferred to salt-free solution for 2 days. The same seedlings and salt concentrations are represented across the displays.
items.explanation: Figure 1 gives 1.8 cm at 6 days for the 6 g/L group, and Figure 2 gives 4.2 cm after recovery. The increase was 4.2 − 1.8 = 2.4 cm.

per_choice.correct: Figure 1 gives 1.8 cm at 6 days for the 6 g/L group, and Figure 2 gives 4.2 cm after recovery. The increase was 4.2 − 1.8 = 2.4 cm.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: A researcher claims that salt permanently damages roots because the 6 g/L group remains shorter than the 0 g/L group after recovery. Which result from Figures 1 and 2 most directly weakens, but does not completely disprove, that claim?
choices: The 6 g/L group had 8 germinated seeds in Table 1.
The 0 g/L group was 5.0 cm at day 6 and 5.8 cm after recovery.
The 6 g/L group increased from 1.8 cm to 4.2 cm after salt was removed.
The 6 g/L group was shorter than the 0 g/L group at day 6.
items.stimulus: Researchers grew bean seeds for 6 days in solutions containing different salt concentrations and measured germination and root growth. They proposed a model in which increasing salinity reduces both processes, with each additional 2 g/L of salt removing the same number of germinated seeds. Table 1 gives germination results, Figure 1 shows mean root length during the experiment, and Figure 2 shows mean root length after seedlings were transferred to salt-free solution for 2 days. The same seedlings and salt concentrations are represented across the displays.
items.explanation: The 6 g/L roots grew 2.4 cm after transfer to salt-free solution, showing that some inhibition was reversible. Their remaining deficit relative to the control means the result does not eliminate the possibility of lasting damage.

per_choice.correct: The 6 g/L roots grew 2.4 cm after transfer to salt-free solution, showing that some inhibition was reversible. Their remaining deficit relative to the control means the result does not eliminate the possibility of lasting damage.
per_choice.trap: C and D support the claim or concern but do not weaken it; B describes control growth and does not show recovery of salt-exposed roots.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which nitrate concentration produced the greatest mean height in Table 1?
choices: 0 mg/L
10 mg/L
20 mg/L
30 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers grew radish seedlings in nutrient solutions containing different nitrate concentrations and measured seedling height over 7 days. The researchers hypothesized that increasing nitrate concentration would increase radish growth. Table 1 shows final mean height and germination percentage for each nitrate concentration. Figure 1 shows height over time for two concentrations, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to grow and measure the seedlings.
items.explanation: The greatest mean height in Table 1 is 14 cm, at 20 mg/L nitrate.

per_choice.correct: The greatest mean height in Table 1 is 14 cm, at 20 mg/L nitrate.
per_choice.trap: Choosing 30 mg/L because it is the highest nitrate concentration rather than reading the greatest height.

items.stem: Which part of Figure 2 was used to measure seedling height?
choices: The seedling tube
The 20 mg/L flask
The 0 mg/L flask
The ruler
items.stimulus: Researchers grew radish seedlings in nutrient solutions containing different nitrate concentrations and measured seedling height over 7 days. The researchers hypothesized that increasing nitrate concentration would increase radish growth. Table 1 shows final mean height and germination percentage for each nitrate concentration. Figure 1 shows height over time for two concentrations, and Figure 2 shows the apparatus used to grow and measure the seedlings.
items.explanation: Figure 2 labels the ruler as the part used to measure height.

per_choice.correct: Figure 2 labels the ruler as the part used to measure height.
per_choice.trap: Choosing a flask or the seedling tube because those parts hold or contain the seedlings.

choices: 0.2 mg/L O2 and 1 mg/L biomass
0.5 mg/L O2 and 1 mg/L biomass
0.5 mg/L O2 and 5 mg/L biomass
1.0 mg/L O2 and 0.5 mg/L biomass
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated the hypothesis that increasing dissolved nitrate concentration always increases oxygen production by algae. Identical algal cultures were supplied with different initial nitrate concentrations and maintained for 5 days under either high-light or low-light conditions; temperature, volume, and starting algal amount were held constant. Table 1 shows final nitrate concentration and algal biomass for the high-light cultures. Figure 1 shows the net dissolved-oxygen change after 24 hours for both light conditions at each initial nitrate concentration. Figure 2 represents the proposed sequence by which nitrate availability could affect dissolved oxygen.
items.explanation: In the high-light series, net oxygen change rises from 10.0 to 10.5 mg/L, a change of 0.5 mg/L. Table 1 shows biomass rising from 30 to 31 mg/L, a change of 1 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: In the high-light series, net oxygen change rises from 10.0 to 10.5 mg/L, a change of 0.5 mg/L. Table 1 shows biomass rising from 30 to 31 mg/L, a change of 1 mg/L.

items.stem: Which initial nitrate concentration most strongly indicates that additional nitrate had become excess rather than limiting under high light, based on both Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: 0 mg/L
2 mg/L
5 mg/L
10 mg/L
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated the hypothesis that increasing dissolved nitrate concentration always increases oxygen production by algae. Identical algal cultures were supplied with different initial nitrate concentrations and maintained for 5 days under either high-light or low-light conditions; temperature, volume, and starting algal amount were held constant. Table 1 shows final nitrate concentration and algal biomass for the high-light cultures. Figure 1 shows the net dissolved-oxygen change after 24 hours for both light conditions at each initial nitrate concentration. Figure 2 represents the proposed sequence by which nitrate availability could affect dissolved oxygen.
items.explanation: At 10 mg/L, Table 1 shows substantial nitrate remaining and only a 1 mg/L biomass increase over the 5 mg/L treatment. Figure 1 likewise shows the high-light oxygen value nearly leveling off from 5 to 10 mg/L.

per_choice.correct: At 10 mg/L, Table 1 shows substantial nitrate remaining and only a 1 mg/L biomass increase over the 5 mg/L treatment. Figure 1 likewise shows the high-light oxygen value nearly leveling off from 5 to 10 mg/L.

items.stem: The researchers want to test whether the near-plateau in the high-light series from 5 to 10 mg/L reflects nitrate saturation rather than a measurement ceiling. Which additional treatment would provide the strongest test, using the relationships shown in Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: A nitrate-free culture under high light with no algae, measuring only the water's oxygen concentration
A 15 mg/L nitrate culture under high light, with final nitrate, biomass, and oxygen measured in the same ways
A 15 mg/L nitrate culture under low light, with only oxygen measured
A 10 mg/L nitrate culture under high light with twice the light intensity, with no biomass measurement
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated the hypothesis that increasing dissolved nitrate concentration always increases oxygen production by algae. Identical algal cultures were supplied with different initial nitrate concentrations and maintained for 5 days under either high-light or low-light conditions; temperature, volume, and starting algal amount were held constant. Table 1 shows final nitrate concentration and algal biomass for the high-light cultures. Figure 1 shows the net dissolved-oxygen change after 24 hours for both light conditions at each initial nitrate concentration. Figure 2 represents the proposed sequence by which nitrate availability could affect dissolved oxygen.
items.explanation: A higher-nitrate, high-light treatment extends the same comparison while measuring both the intermediate biomass and the final oxygen response. If oxygen and biomass remain near the 5-to-10 mg/L values, saturation is supported; if they rise, the apparent plateau may have reflected the tested range.

per_choice.correct: A higher-nitrate, high-light treatment extends the same comparison while measuring both the intermediate biomass and the final oxygen response. If oxygen and biomass remain near the 5-to-10 mg/L values, saturation is supported; if they rise, the apparent plateau may have reflected the tested range.
per_choice.trap: Choice C changes light while extending nitrate, so it cannot isolate saturation; choice D changes light and omits the pathway intermediate; choice A removes the algal pathway rather than testing the plateau.

items.stem: Assuming each high-light series segment in Figure 1 is linear, what pair of values would be estimated at an initial nitrate concentration of 7.5 mg/L for net oxygen change and algal biomass, respectively, using Figure 1 and Table 1?
choices: 5.25 mg/L O2 and 30.0 mg/L biomass
10.25 mg/L O2 and 30.5 mg/L biomass
10.50 mg/L O2 and 31.0 mg/L biomass
15.00 mg/L O2 and 35.0 mg/L biomass
items.stimulus: Researchers investigated the hypothesis that increasing dissolved nitrate concentration always increases oxygen production by algae. Identical algal cultures were supplied with different initial nitrate concentrations and maintained for 5 days under either high-light or low-light conditions; temperature, volume, and starting algal amount were held constant. Table 1 shows final nitrate concentration and algal biomass for the high-light cultures. Figure 1 shows the net dissolved-oxygen change after 24 hours for both light conditions at each initial nitrate concentration. items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which evaluation of the stated bacterial-conversion model is best supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?
choices: The model is untested because only the final NH3 concentration, not any intermediate concentration, was measured.
The model is supported solely because the discharge NH3 concentration is lower than the intake concentration.
The model is contradicted because NO3− does not increase until after the biofilter.
The model is supported: at the biofilter, NH3 decreases while NO3− increases under oxygen-rich conditions, although the data alone do not prove that bacteria caused the change.
items.stimulus: Researchers evaluated a model in which aerobic bacteria in a wastewater biofilter convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrate (NO3−), with the biofilter predicted to be the main conversion stage. Water from one treatment stream was sampled at five successive stages, and dissolved oxygen (DO), NH3, and NO3− were measured. Table 1 gives DO and NH3 for each stage, while Figure 1 gives NH3 and NO3− concentrations at the numbered stages. Figure 2 shows the order of the stages; the numbered positions in Figure 1 correspond to that order.
items.explanation: At the transition into and through the biofilter, NH3 falls from 16 to 7 mg/L while NO3− rises from 0.8 to 6.2 mg/L; Table 1 also shows 6.4 mg/L DO there. This supports the predicted pattern but does not by itself establish bacterial causation.

per_choice.correct: At the transition into and through the biofilter, NH3 falls from 16 to 7 mg/L while NO3− rises from 0.8 to 6.2 mg/L; Table 1 also shows 6.4 mg/L DO there. This supports the predicted pattern but does not by itself establish bacterial causation.
per_choice.trap: The last choice uses the correct overall decrease but ignores where the decrease and nitrate increase occur; the third choice mistakes the small post-biofilter nitrate increase for evidence against conversion in the biofilter.

items.stem: What percentage of the intake NH3 concentration has been removed by the time the water reaches the biofilter stage? Use Table 1.
items.stimulus: Researchers evaluated a model in which aerobic bacteria in a wastewater biofilter convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrate (NO3−), with the biofilter predicted to be the main conversion stage. Water from one treatment stream was sampled at five successive stages, and dissolved oxygen (DO), NH3, and NO3− were measured. Table 1 gives DO and NH3 for each stage, while Figure 1 gives NH3 and NO3− concentrations at the numbered stages. Figure 2 shows the order of the stages; the numbered positions in Figure 1 correspond to that order.
items.explanation: NH3 decreases from 18 mg/L at intake to 7 mg/L at the biofilter, so the decrease is 11 mg/L. The percentage removed is 11/18 × 100 = 61.1%.

per_choice.correct: NH3 decreases from 18 mg/L at intake to 7 mg/L at the biofilter, so the decrease is 11 mg/L. The percentage removed is 11/18 × 100 = 61.1%.
per_choice.trap: 50.0% results from using the biofilter value as the denominator; 66.7% comes from comparing the decrease with the biofilter value rather than the intake value.

items.stem: According to Table 1 and Figure 1, which transition shows both the greatest decrease in NH3 and the greatest increase in NO3−?
choices: Aeration to biofilter
Biofilter to settling
Intake to aeration
Settling to discharge
items.stimulus: Researchers evaluated a model in which aerobic bacteria in a wastewater biofilter convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrate (NO3−), with the biofilter predicted to be the main conversion stage. Water from one treatment stream was sampled at five successive stages, and dissolved oxygen (DO), NH3, and NO3− were measured. Table 1 gives DO and NH3 for each stage, while Figure 1 gives NH3 and NO3− concentrations at the numbered stages. Figure 2 shows the order of the stages; the numbered positions in Figure 1 correspond to that order.
items.explanation: From aeration to biofilter, NH3 decreases from 16 to 7 mg/L, a 9 mg/L decrease, while NO3− increases from 0.8 to 6.2 mg/L, a 5.4 mg/L increase. Both changes exceed those at the other transitions.

per_choice.correct: From aeration to biofilter, NH3 decreases from 16 to 7 mg/L, a 9 mg/L decrease, while NO3− increases from 0.8 to 6.2 mg/L, a 5.4 mg/L increase. Both changes exceed those at the other transitions.
per_choice.trap: The intake-to-aeration transition has the largest DO increase, but DO is not the requested quantity; the later transitions can look important because NO3− is already high there.

items.tests: Whether a stated hypothesis is supported, contradicted, or untested by the results.

items.stem: Which comparison would best test whether the biofilter, rather than merely the passage of time through the treatment system, is responsible for the major NH3-to-NO3− change?
choices: Increase aeration while leaving the biofilter in place and compare the resulting discharge with the original intake.
Measure the same discharge sample twice to determine whether its NH3 concentration is stable.
Compare intake water with discharge water, without changing the treatment path.
Route a comparable stream through aeration and settling but bypass the biofilter, then measure NH3 and NO3− at discharge.
items.stimulus: Researchers evaluated a model in which aerobic bacteria in a wastewater biofilter convert ammonia (NH3) to nitrate (NO3−), with the biofilter predicted to be the main conversion stage. Water from one treatment stream was sampled at five successive stages, and dissolved oxygen (DO), NH3, and NO3− were measured. Table 1 gives DO and NH3 for each stage, while Figure 1 gives NH3 and NO3− concentrations at the numbered stages. Figure 2 shows the order of the stages; the numbered positions in Figure 1 correspond to that order.
items.explanation: A stream that follows the same general path but bypasses the biofilter isolates the presence of the biofilter as the key difference. Measuring both NH3 and NO3− tests the predicted conversion rather than only total removal.

per_choice.correct: A stream that follows the same general path but bypasses the biofilter isolates the presence of the biofilter as the key difference. Measuring both NH3 and NO3− tests the predicted conversion rather than only total removal.
per_choice.trap: The first and second choices provide no biofilter comparison, while the third changes aeration and therefore introduces another possible cause of any change.
